summary: Automatic host fencing slice 4c: the pool owns its cluster. Slice 4b built the watchdog engine and nothing armed anywhere, because a diskless sbd has no quorum to lose unless a Corosync/Pacemaker cluster exists and Nex Core formed none. This slice makes Nex Core form and maintain one resource-free Corosync/Pacemaker cluster per pool, for pools of three or more ready hosts with Host fencing on and NO clustered-storage repository, so such a pool arms by itself. Owner decisions, 2026-09-22: build this for plain pools first, leaving clustered-storage pools reporting 'not armed' with the reason until a separate GFS2/DLM slice; and keep Host fencing ON by default, over both the implementer's and the reviewer's recommendation of off-until-hardware-proven, which makes closing every known way default-on could reset a healthy host this slice's job. THE NODELIST IS DERIVED, NEVER A SECOND SOURCE OF TRUTH: every host renders the pool's corosync.conf from the membership it already holds, with ring addresses from PoolMember.peer_origin, node names that are the durable host IDs (what corosync-quorumtool reads back and what pcmk_host_* already matches) and node IDs that are a stable digest of the host ID and are never reused for another host. No cluster record is created and nothing is added for a Controller to keep or recover. RenderStorageCluster and the pool cluster became two callers of one renderer and ONE WRITER, writeCorosyncConfig, which refuses to take a corosync.conf over from the other consumer. NOTHING COMES UP ARMED: corosync and pacemaker are started by the reconcile and NEVER enabled at boot, and a host that has just booted disables sbd before that start. This removes the only hazard in the feature with no failure behind it — a host whose cluster starts alone after a site power cut, or the last host of a pool rebooting, is inquorate from its first moment and under no-quorum-policy=suicide would reset itself in a loop with the whole pool healthy. SBD_DELAY_START=yes and votequorum wait_for_all are the second and third lines of defence, not the first. ARMING IS A ROLLOUT CORE RUNS, ONE HOST AT A TIME, WITH NO GRANT TO KEEP: a host arms only after it has watched one unchanged Corosync membership, quorate and containing every host of the cluster, for a full PoolWatchdogBound, and only when it is its turn — and the turn is DERIVED from the membership (the first ready host, in host-ID order, that has not reported itself armed), so there is nothing durable to add, nothing to resume and no way for two hosts to hold it at once. The host whose turn it is restarts its own cluster services, which is the only way Debian's RefuseManualStart sbd.service can start, while the others stay quorate; RestartPoolClusterForArming refuses any CIB with a resource in it, so this can never become the thing that restarts Corosync under a mounted clustered filesystem. A host that cannot arm holds the turn and the rollout stops there, visibly, with that host's own reason: fewer armed hosts is less protection, never a false proof. CLUSTERED STORAGE AND WATCHDOG FENCING EXCLUDE EACH OTHER IN CORE, BOTH WAYS AND TESTED: a pool with a clustered repository is never given a watchdog cluster and reports 'this pool runs clustered storage; watchdog fencing for it is not available yet'; creating a clustered repository on a pool whose hosts are armed is refused, naming Host fencing off as the way out; and under both, the single-writer rule on corosync.conf means the interlock does not depend on an intent check being right. The reason is measured: clustered storage writes no-quorum-policy=freeze, and slice 4b measured a freeze host still running two minutes after it was partitioned. A MEMBERSHIP CHANGE IS A RELOAD: the nodelist is rewritten and corosync-cfgtool -R applied, so Nex's ready count and votequorum's expected votes move together without restarting a peer that is feeding a watchdog. MAINTENANCE MODE IS THE SUPPORTED WAY TO DO DISRUPTIVE WORK: a host entering maintenance leaves the cluster after the pool's record says it is not armed, and a three-host pool that loses one has no majority side, so the whole pool disarms through the recorded path and reports it — deliberately, rather than reaching for last_man_standing or a reduced expected_votes, which would buy availability by reintroducing the split-brain the feature exists to prevent. THE RING RUNS ON THE MANAGEMENT NETWORK, so a staged management-network change on an armed host is a partition of that host: Core refuses to stage or apply one while this host is feeding a watchdog, and the guide and the setting say so. THE WITHDRAWAL WINDOW IS CLOSED BY A REJOIN RULE, NOT A FRESHNESS RULE: PoolWatchdogArmed.armed_at makes a new spell of arming a different record, so a host that stopped and started its watchdog replicates a change, and a proving host refuses a proof against a target that joined its Corosync partition after the last armed record it holds. A freshness rule on observed_at would have been wrong in the other direction, because a legitimately partitioned host cannot refresh its report either. Four of slice 4b's independent-review findings close with it: N1 (cold start), N2 (the postinst now guards on the '# Managed by Nex Core' marker in /etc/default/sbd, so an ordinary package upgrade cannot silently disarm an armed pool), N3 (the arming pass moved onto its own tick ahead of the cluster pass, so notice latency is bounded by the probe interval rather than by a conversation with a management controller), N4 (maintenance), N5 (an Observed quorum reading with no ring identifier counts as an observation gap rather than degrading the flap detector silently) and N6 (the gap is half the minimum bound rather than a quarter, which leaves real margin over the reading cadence). Nex Controller relays PoolFenceSummary.cluster verbatim and keeps nothing. REVISED AFTER INDEPENDENT REVIEW, which found no false-proof path but three confirmed defects and two plausible ones, all fixed here with regression tests that model what the earlier fakes flattened. F1: the cold-start defence rested on the arming pass having reached the master first, which a host booting after a site power cut cannot do; sbd is still enabled from the last time that host armed, on a corosync.service.requires edge, so it came up armed and alone. ApplyPoolCluster now disables sbd immediately before it starts the cluster, unconditionally, and a host that is not feeding anything disables it even when it cannot record the withdrawal. F2: the rejoin rule refused EVERY proof after any membership event, because a Corosync ring change was treated as every present host rejoining and the only re-confirmation in the tree was a test helper - so the pool's own arming rollout poisoned itself. A window this host did not watch is now kept apart from a membership event it did watch, and the producing half is production code: an armed host that finds itself on a membership it has not verified on re-verifies and re-reports, which moves armed_at, which is what a survivor reads; a settled pool still writes nothing. PoolWatchdogUsable applies the same rejoin condition as the proof, so readiness and the promotion cannot disagree. F3 and F5: turning Host fencing off, or maintenance on one host, reset a healthy host - disarming has latency and expected votes do not shrink because somebody else left, so the last host standing was inquorate and still feeding. PoolWatchdogArmed.feeding now reports the device separately from armed; nobody leaves the cluster while any host of it is still feeding; one host at a time puts its device down by restarting its own cluster while the rest stay quorate; and a drained host stays in every survivor's nodelist until its own record says it has stopped feeding. F4: stonith-watchdog-timeout is written only when the pool's own records say EVERY node is armed and Pacemaker also reports have-watchdog, because have-watchdog is cluster-wide and goes true as soon as the first host runs sbd. The teardown re-measurement then found the same Pacemaker rule in the other direction - the whole cluster shut down as the last host put its watchdog down - so the master now UNSETS the bound as soon as the pool stops being fully armed, which the lab confirms keeps the cluster up through a teardown. REVISED AGAIN after the reviewer's verification of rev 2, which confirmed one HIGH remaining: the first teardown restart still happened while stonith-watchdog-timeout was set on a node with no sbd - the fatal Pacemaker condition, and the exact ordering the rev-2 lab captured resetting a healthy host. Rev 3 removes the mechanism rather than ordering around it. stonith-watchdog-timeout is NOT WRITTEN AT ALL and is REMOVED wherever it is found, and a host refuses to start a cluster whose CIB still carries one. The property is the quorate side's wait before Pacemaker recovers RESOURCES, and a pool's cluster has none by construction; Nex's own 60 s proof bound, which gates promotion, is independent of the CIB. Two orderings had already been tried and each left another ordinary event that puts an unarmed node on the cluster: forming it, the rollout, a teardown, and a host rebooting back into an armed pool - the last of which the rebuilt harness exposed only after the CIB was modelled in it rather than stubbed out. The nested lab then settled it decisively: with NO bound anywhere, three hosts armed one at a time with nobody resetting and Pacemaker setting have-watchdog itself, and a partitioned minority host still reset at 17.9 s - the same figure as with the property set - with its own journal showing pacemaker-controld 'emerg: Signaling sbd to panic the system: Quorum lost'. The teardown, maintenance and a host rebooting back into an armed pool were then all re-measured IN THE CODE'S OWN ORDER with nothing unset by hand, and every one is clean. Also in rev 3: the teardown turn waits until the bound is observed unset from the CIB (not from a record) and until this host's departure would leave every still-feeding peer quorate, so a host lost mid-teardown no longer stalls it for ever; a stalled teardown is reported as degraded and names the host it is waiting for; an armed host also re-confirms once per proof bound, so a single missed reading on a PROVING host no longer blocks proofs against hosts that never moved; and the dead poolClusterHaveWatchdog is deleted. REV 4, after the reviewer's verification of rev 3 ratified the removal of stonith-watchdog-timeout (Decision: project owner, 2026-09-22, recorded in the plan: the property's only function is to let the quorate side assume a watchdog-only node is down so it can recover that node's RESOURCES, and a pool's cluster is resource-free by construction, so it bought nothing while the lab measured it costing a healthy-host reset). R1, named as the last plausible way default-on could reset a healthy host, is CLOSED BY MEASUREMENT: a host that starts this cluster alone - peers down, suicide already in its persisted CIB, sbd disabled - does NOT panic, because Pacemaker refuses to apply the policy to a cluster that has never had quorum and says so ('Resetting no-quorum-policy to stop: cluster has never had quorum'). votequorum's wait_for_all: 1 is what makes a lone host's membership never-quorate, so the property added to stop a starting minority forming a false majority is also what holds the suicide back on a cold start; it held with stonith-enabled true and false over 165 s with an unchanged boot id. R2: the contradictory API.md and plan text is fixed - slice 4b's 30 s bound and its per-host-BMC-STONITH-on-this-cluster claim are marked superseded, and the unimplemented 'refuses to start a cluster whose CIB carries the property' claim is replaced by what the code does (a host will not RESTART while it is there; nothing can strip a CIB before Pacemaker runs, so an inherited one is repaired by the master once the cluster is up). stonith-enabled was measured both ways: false silences Pacemaker's permanent no-STONITH-resources errors and an armed host still self-fenced at 17.9 s, but true is kept because every other partition measurement was taken under it and the fence firing is the one property not to risk on a single run; the log-noise cost is documented and the change is an owner decision. R3: a teardown blocked by a lost host now reports 'armed - teardown blocked by <host>' rather than progress, with the guide telling the operator it finishes when the host returns or is ejected, and the regression kills the host BEFORE any turn, which is the ordering the fix was written for. R4: the blind-window and teardown-arithmetic checks are load-bearing, and a new test covers the PoolClusterBoundSet gate against a CIB from elsewhere. R5: the cluster stop is bounded at 20 s and on timeout the host stays armed and feeding and says so - sbd is never signalled. R6: poolClusterArmedCount and poolQuorumWhole deleted. R7: the over-read evidence note is corrected. REV 5, the reviewer's final pass: the watchdog-expiry path is now PROVEN on the emulated device. SIGSTOP on an armed host's sbd processes, with the pool quorate throughout so no no-quorum-policy could apply and Pacemaker unable to signal a stopped daemon, reset that host within 8 s against a 5 s device timeout, its two survivors untouched, and its previous boot's journal ends mid-stream with no emerg, no panic and no shutdown trace - the signature of the device resetting the machine. That closes the one remaining false-proof gap in mechanism and narrows the acceptance gate to 'no PHYSICAL watchdog model is proven'. The plan's gates and the guide's Limits now carry it, the guide distinguishes the two things that reset a host, the softdog and no-watchdog rows say the host still reboots with a minority and only cannot be PROVED excluded, the double-failure consequence is in the guide and beside the Host fencing switch, the R3 wording says reporting plus ejection rather than unblocking, and the 20 s stop bound has its own vmhost test that fails when the bound is widened.

guide.reason: A pool of three or more hosts without clustered storage now arms by itself, which is behaviour an operator must meet before it can reset a host. docs/guide/pool-authority-and-recovery.md gains 'The pool's own cluster' (what it is, that the operator neither creates nor configures it, that the pool's hosts are armed one at a time and the line says 'arming host 2 of 3', and that the ring runs on the management network so a staged management-network change is refused on an armed host), 'Maintenance mode is the supported way to do disruptive work' (a host entering maintenance leaves the cluster cleanly and a three-host pool that loses one disarms entirely and says so), and five new rows in the watchdog-line table: waiting for the cluster to settle, waiting for another host's arming turn, a clustered-storage pool, a pool above the tested ceiling, and a pool whose cluster is not up yet. The obsolete limit 'Nex Core does not yet form a pool's cluster, and writes none of its properties — in practice nothing arms by itself yet' is removed, because it is no longer true; the clustered-storage half of it is kept and made specific, because it still is. Rev 5 adds: the two reset mechanisms and what each has been tested on; that a softdog-only or watchdog-less host is still a member of the pool's cluster and still reboots with a minority, and only cannot be proved excluded; the double-failure consequence in a three-host pool and that maintenance mode on the first host is the supported path for planned work on two; and what an operator does when a lost host blocks a teardown (wait for it, or eject it).

api.reason: No new route. PoolFenceSummary gains cluster (PoolFenceCluster{state, detail, armed, total, arming_host_id}), the master's memory-only observation over the membership it owns, derived on every report and never stored; state is closed to off, not_available, forming, arming, armed and degraded. PoolWatchdogArmed gains armed_at, the host's own clock at the moment it started feeding a device, carried over unchanged while it goes on feeding the same one, so that a host which stopped and started its watchdog produces a record that differs from the one before — an identical record is never written or replicated, and a survivor would otherwise be unable to tell 'armed since before it left' from 'was armed once, and has been up unarmed since'. It rides the existing POST /api/v1/pool/advertise watchdog_armed key with the same validation and the same recorded-in-the-calling-member's-own-row rule. New capability pool-watchdog-cluster-v1: a master without it forms no cluster and reports no cluster field, which a client shows as no cluster line rather than as a cluster that is off; a member too old to report armed_at leaves it zero, which is never read as a re-arm, so the proving host's rejoin check refuses after a rejoin until the record changes for another reason — the safe direction. Two refusals are new and are Core's: POST /api/v1/pools/{id}/storage-cluster's apply is refused on a pool whose hosts are armed or whose watchdog cluster Nex Core is forming, and POST /api/v1/hosts/{id}/network refuses to stage or apply while this host is feeding a watchdog. Both are definite failed results carrying Core's own sentence and naming the way out. All three machine-readable contracts and the generated reference are regenerated; docs/API.md gains 'The pool's own cluster, and the arming rollout' and its arming section is corrected where 4b's 'it never restarts a running cluster' is now 'it never restarts a cluster that is running resources, checked against the CIB'. PoolWatchdogArmed also gains feeding: whether the device is still being fed, which is not the same question as armed. armed is what the pool may rest a proof on and goes false the moment the pool decides this host should stop; the device is released only when that host's cluster next stops. Every other host needs the difference, because a host that leaves the cluster while a peer is still feeding can take that peer below quorum. It rides the same advertise key with the same validation, and armed_at is now bounded (a host cannot claim to have armed in the future) like every field beside it. stonith-watchdog-timeout is no longer part of the contract Nex Core writes: it is not set, it is removed where found, and a host will not start a cluster whose CIB carries it. docs/API.md says why, and names the slice it belongs to.

roadmap.reason: The published roadmap describes shipped capability at a coarser grain than one fencing slice. The plan records what 4c settled, marks each acceptance gate met-by-test, met-in-nested-lab or OPEN, and keeps the two open gates explicit: physical-hardware evidence, and arming a pool that runs clustered storage.

state.reason: The pool's Corosync/Pacemaker cluster is derived state, not a record. Every host renders its own corosync.conf from the master's durable membership, which already replicates: the node list is the pool's ready hosts, the ring addresses are the peer origins the membership already carries, the node names are the durable host IDs and the node IDs are a pure function of those host IDs. Whose turn it is to arm is derived the same way, from each host's own armed report in that membership, so the rollout needs no grant, no job record and nothing to resume. Nothing was added to the Controller: it relays PoolFenceSummary.cluster verbatim, displays it, and keeps no cluster state, no node list, no arming turn and no quorum reading. Delete the Controller, install a fresh one and connect the master, and the pool's cluster, its arming and every host's armed report come back from the hosts with the workloads never having stopped.
state.record: Durable, on the pool master, in pool-peer.json: PoolMembership.members (each host's host_id, status, maintenance and peer_origin, which together are the cluster's node list) and PoolMember.watchdog_armed including its new armed_at, plus PoolMembership.host_fencing_disabled, all of which already existed and already replicate to every member in the signed authority replica. The rendered /etc/corosync/corosync.conf and the CIB properties on each host are projections of that record and are rewritten from it on every reconcile pass; losing them loses nothing. A fresh Controller recovers all of it by reading the master's reported inventory, exactly as it recovers the membership itself; PoolFenceSummary.cluster is recomputed by the master on every report and is never stored anywhere.

verification.method: Go unit tests against fakes for systemd, corosync, the CIB and sbd; in-process three-host and four-host pool labs over the real mutual-TLS peer transport, on a harness that models sbd's three states (enabled and not running, feeding, off), the latency of a disarm, quorum moving as hosts leave, AND the CIB's stonith-watchdog-timeout together with Pacemaker's response to it - stubbing that property out is what hid the reset the lab had already measured. After every simulated tick the harness applies both measured rules: Pacemaker's emerg shutdown when the bound is set and a node has no sbd, and sbd's reset when a feeding host cannot see a majority. Every teardown, boot and reboot test asserts both sets are empty. React unit tests. And a disposable nested three-host QEMU/KVM laboratory with real corosync 3, pacemaker 3.0 and sbd. RESULTS, all run in this working tree on 2026-09-22 after the rev-3 fixes: go build ./... PASS; go vet ./internal/... PASS; go test -count=1 ./internal/... PASS (all packages); go test -race -count=1 ./internal/agent/ ./internal/vmhost/ PASS; tsc --noEmit PASS; every web/src/*.test.mjs PASS; python3 scripts/generate_api.py --check PASS; python3 -m unittest discover -s tests PASS (394); python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -p 'test_repository_privacy.py' PASS; python3 scripts/check_docs.py --worktree PASS; gofmt clean on every file this slice touched. NESTED LABORATORY, the QA evidence page docs/qa/2026-09-22-automatic-host-fencing.md - 28 steps, each with every host's real boot id, is-active and is-enabled for corosync/sbd/pacemaker, the watchdog sysfs state, the full corosync-quorumtool output, the cluster properties read back, and each node's pacemaker journal; driven IN THE CODE'S OWN ORDER with nothing unset or ordered by hand, and carrying a provenance header that says so. MEASURED: the cluster forms quorate with nothing armed; three hosts arm one at a time with no boot id changing, all three quorate at every step, have-watchdog set by Pacemaker itself, and no stonith-watchdog-timeout anywhere; a partitioned minority host reset at 17.9 s - the same as with the property set - with both survivors quorate and unchanged, and its own journal reading 'emerg: Signaling sbd to panic the system: Quorum lost'; the ordered teardown put all three devices down one at a time with the cluster UP AND QUORATE ON ALL THREE HOSTS throughout and nobody resetting; maintenance on one host of three did the same and left a quorate two; and a host rebooting back into a fully armed pool rejoined UNARMED with the other two armed and running, and nobody reset - the fourth ordinary path to an unarmed node on the cluster, and the one the harness exposed. EARLIER CAPTURES, kept with provenance headers marking them superseded: evidence-scenarios.json (rev 2 - formation, rollout, both partitions, a single-host reboot and a whole-pool cold start, all still valid; its maintenance-settled step is the reset the old ordering caused) and evidence-teardown.json (rev 2's teardown, which was made safe BY HAND and is not evidence about the code's order). REV 4 ADDS the QA evidence page docs/qa/2026-09-22-automatic-host-fencing.md, two hand-issued measurements with their journal lines: R1, a lone host starting the pool's cluster with suicide persisted, which did not panic over 165 s and whose journal names Pacemaker's own reason; and R2, stonith-enabled=false, which silenced the permanent scheduler errors while an armed host still self-fenced at 17.9 s. Both were driven by hand because the batch step for R1 was itself wedged by the hung `systemctl stop pacemaker` this slice reports. Reverts re-checked for the three fixes the reviewer found reverting clean: the ArmedAt time bucket, the teardown arithmetic and the PoolClusterBoundSet gate now each fail a named test when reverted. REV 5 ADDS the QA evidence page docs/qa/2026-09-22-automatic-host-fencing.md: the watchdog-expiry measurement described above, with boot IDs before and after, the device's sysfs state, sbd's process states under SIGSTOP, the survivors' boot IDs and the absence of any shutdown trace in the victim's previous-boot journal.
untested: No physical watchdog device of any model has been read, armed or expired, and no physical host has been reset.

The watchdog-expiry path is proven only on QEMU's emulated i6300esb, and only by stopping sbd rather than by hanging a kernel. No physical chipset or BMC watchdog of any model has been read, armed or expired, on any machine, under any load; and a real kernel hang was not staged, so what is shown is that the device expires and resets when nothing feeds it, not that a hung kernel reaches that state on real hardware.

No GFS2 filesystem and no DLM was mounted in any measurement, so nothing here is evidence about a clustered-storage pool. That is also where stonith-watchdog-timeout belongs, and what it does to DLM recovery is unmeasured.

The agent binary was not run inside the laboratory guests. The sequences measured are the commands Nex Core issues, in the order it issues them; the code that decides WHEN is covered by Go tests only. Most of the defects independent review found across four rounds were in that 'when'.
No watchdog proof and no promotion ran in the laboratory. What was measured is the precondition: partitions in which the target reset itself and the survivors stayed quorate.

Not exercised in the laboratory: an agent restart or upgrade on an armed host, a package upgrade of an armed pool, a join, an eject, a master change, creating a clustered-storage repository while armed, maintenance in a pool of four or five, and a teardown blocked by a lost host. Each is covered by a Go test.

A host that HAS been quorate and then starts its cluster alone after a reboot was not staged separately: Pacemaker reported 'never had quorum' for the new corosync membership in the case measured, and quorum history is not persisted, but the distinction was not exercised.
Whether sbd treats a pacemaker stopped under a live corosync as a graceful shutdown is uncharacterised. The 20 s bound and the report cover the stall; they do not measure sbd's behaviour in it.
stonith-enabled=false has one run behind it. It is not the shipped setting.

SBD_DELAY_START=yes is rendered but its effect was not isolated: the cold-start protection measured comes from nothing being enabled at boot, from ApplyPoolCluster disabling sbd before it starts a cluster, and from wait_for_all making a lone membership never-quorate.
The 60 s proof bound and SBD_WATCHDOG_TIMEOUT=5 rest on nested runs at a two-second poll, and must be re-measured on physical hardware.
The re-confirmation writes one small record per armed host per proof bound, so a settled pool re-signs its authority replica about once a minute per host. Its cost at larger pool sizes is unmeasured.
The new cluster states were reviewed in the React unit tests only; no browser capture was taken in this slice.
Every outstanding item from slices 1 to 4b remains outstanding, including that no physical management controller has been contacted and no host has been powered off.
